title: PagedAttention: the core memory trick
description: vLLM's PagedAttention borrows the operating system's virtual-memory paging idea: the key-value cache is split into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand instead of one wasteful contiguous reservation per request. This nearly eliminates memory fragmentation, so far more concurrent requests fit on the same GPU. It is the reason vLLM serves many simultaneous users where naive servers choke.

demo.program:
block=16
print(f'KV cache in {block}-token blocks, allocated on demand')
print('result: ~0 fragmentation, more concurrent requests')
demo.expected_output:
KV cache in 16-token blocks, allocated on demand
result: ~0 fragmentation, more concurrent requests

title: Continuous batching of requests
description: Instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, vLLM's scheduler adds new requests to the running batch the moment any request completes (iteration-level scheduling). GPUs stay busy at all times and short requests do not wait behind long ones. This is the second pillar of vLLM's throughput, alongside PagedAttention.

demo.program:
print('scheduler: token-by-token, new requests join mid-batch')
print('GPU never idles waiting for the longest request')

scheduler: token-by-token, new requests join mid-batch
GPU never idles waiting for the longest request

title: OpenAI-compatible server in one command
description: Running `vllm serve <model>` starts an HTTP server with OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions and /v1/completions endpoints, so existing clients work unchanged. It is the fastest path from a Hugging Face model ID to a production-style API on your own GPU, with no code changes in the client.

title: Tensor parallelism across GPUs
description: The --tensor-parallel-size flag shards model weights across multiple GPUs so models too big for one card still serve fast. vLLM handles the collective communication, and throughput scales because attention and MLP layers split cleanly. Multi-GPU serving becomes a flag, not a rewrite.

title: GPU memory utilization tuning
description: --gpu-memory-utilization (default 0.90) sets what fraction of GPU memory vLLM may use for the KV cache and weights. Raising it fits more concurrent requests; lowering it leaves room for other processes. It is the first knob to turn when balancing throughput against sharing the card.

title: Quantization support: AWQ, GPTQ, FP8
description: vLLM natively serves AWQ and GPTQ 4-bit quantized models and FP8 models, loading the compressed weights directly without a separate conversion step. Quantized serving multiplies effective VRAM, so a 70B model can serve on fewer cards. The --quantization flag selects the scheme explicitly when autodetect is unsure.

title: Prefix caching for repeated prompts
description: With --enable-prefix-caching, vLLM reuses computed key-value blocks for shared prompt prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples), skipping recomputation for every request that starts the same way. Chat applications with long system prompts see large speedups because the prefix is computed once and shared.

title: Structured outputs: JSON mode and grammars
description: vLLM supports guided decoding: JSON schema mode, regex, and grammar-constrained generation that guarantee the output matches a required shape. The constraint is enforced during sampling, so no post-hoc parsing or retries are needed. This makes local models reliable for tool-calling pipelines.

title: Chat templates from the tokenizer

t: Max model length and context control
title: Max model length and context control
description: --max-model-len caps the context window (prompt + output) the server accepts, which directly controls KV cache sizing. Lowering it when you only need short answers frees memory for more concurrent requests. It is the main lever for fitting long-context models onto limited VRAM.

title: Streaming responses with SSE
description: The server streams tokens as server-sent events, so clients render answers word-by-word instead of waiting for completion. Streaming works with the OpenAI client libraries unchanged (stream=True) and is essential for interactive chat latency perception. vLLM's scheduler makes streaming efficient even under load.

title: Graceful shutdown and request draining
description: SIGTERM handling drains in-flight requests before the server exits, so rolling restarts in production do not cut off users mid-answer. Combined with health endpoints, orchestrators can replace vLLM pods with zero dropped completions. It is the detail that makes vLLM production-grade rather than demo-grade.
